modules.title: Binary & Number Bases
modules.why: Computers count in binary. Reading bits, converting between binary, decimal, and hex, and understanding octal unlocks networking, memory, permissions, and cryptography topics across the catalog.

slides.heading: Bits and bytes
slides.lede: Every photo, video, and program is stored as bits. Learn what a bit is and the whole digital world starts making sense.
slides.narration: This lecture defines bits and bytes, counts in powers of two, and explains why computers chose binary in the first place.

slides.heading: The smallest pieces
bullets: A bit is one binary digit: 0 or 1. It is the smallest possible piece of information.
A byte is 8 bits. One byte can represent 256 different values, from 0 to 255.
Computers use binary because hardware is built from switches: on or off, current or no current.
Counting bits goes in powers of two: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256...
Those powers appear everywhere: 256 IP values per octet, 8-bit file permissions, 64-bit processors.
slides.narration: Bits are binary digits, bytes are groups of eight, and powers of two are the counting rhythm of all computing hardware.

slides.heading: Powers of two
slides.walkthrough: Each row doubles the last: that is what raising 2 to a power means. 2^8 = 256 is the key fact — one byte holds 256 distinct values, which is why an IPv4 octet ranges from 0 to 255.
slides.narration: Memorize the powers of two up to 2^8. They are the multiplication table of computing, and 256 is the most important number on it.

slides.heading: From bit to byte

diagram.title: From bit to byte
diagram.note: A nibble is half a byte — exactly one hex digit, which is why hex and binary fit together so neatly.

slides.narration: Bits stack into nibbles, nibbles into bytes, and bytes into the 256 values that address memory, color pixels, and number network octets.

slides.heading: Try it: count the values
slides.text: How many different values can 4 bits represent? (Hint: it is 2^4.) Then: how many values can 2 bytes represent?
slides.narration: Apply the powers of two: 4 bits give 16 values, and 2 bytes give 65,536. This pattern answers every how many values question.

lectures.title: Binary to decimal, step by step

slides.heading: Binary to decimal, step by step
slides.lede: Binary looks alien until you see the trick: each position is just a power of two. Add the ones that are switched on.
slides.narration: This lecture teaches positional notation and works a full binary-to-decimal conversion, digit by digit.

slides.heading: Positional notation
bullets: In decimal, 237 means 2 hundreds + 3 tens + 7 ones. Each position is worth ten times the one to its right.
Binary works identically, but each position is worth two times the one to its right: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16...
The rightmost position is always the ones place (2^0 = 1) in every base.
To convert: write each position's value under its digit, keep the values under the 1s, and add them up.
A 0 means that position contributes nothing. Only the 1s count.
slides.narration: Binary is positional notation with powers of two instead of powers of ten. Write the place values, keep the ones under the 1s, and add.

slides.heading: Worked: 1011 to decimal
slides.walkthrough: Label each digit with its place value: 8, 4, 2, 1 from left to right. The 1s sit under 8, 2, and 1; the 0 sits under 4 and contributes nothing. Add the kept values: 8 + 2 + 1 = 11.
slides.narration: Follow the three steps: label place values, keep only those under 1s, and add. Binary 1011 is decimal 11.

slides.heading: The conversion recipe

diagram.title: The conversion recipe
diagram.note: The same recipe converts any base to decimal — only the place values change.

slides.narration: The recipe never changes: place values, keep the active ones, add. Master it in binary and hex becomes a small variation.

slides.heading: Try it: convert 11010
slides.text: Convert binary 11010 to decimal using the recipe. Place values are 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. (Answer: 26.)
slides.narration: Work 11010 by hand: label, keep, add. Checking against 26 confirms the method before hex raises the stakes.

lectures.title: Hex, octal, and going the other way

slides.heading: Hex, octal, and going the other way
slides.lede: Hexadecimal is binary's compact cousin: one hex digit per four bits. Learn the grouping trick and long bit strings shrink.
slides.narration: This lecture converts decimal to binary by repeated division, then introduces hexadecimal and octal as shorthand for bit groups.

slides.heading: New bases
bullets: Decimal to binary: divide by 2 repeatedly, keep the remainders, read them bottom-up.
Hexadecimal is base 16. Digits are 0-9 then A-F, where A=10 through F=15.
One hex digit holds exactly 4 bits, so binary converts to hex by grouping digits in fours.
Octal is base 8, digits 0-7, grouping bits in threes. You will meet it in Unix file permissions.
Hex shows up in memory addresses, color codes (#FF0000 is red), and MAC addresses.
slides.narration: Repeated division converts decimal to binary; grouping converts binary to hex and octal. Hex is everywhere addresses and colors appear.

slides.heading: Worked: 13 to binary to hex

code.code:
13 / 2 = 6 remainder 1
 6 / 2 = 3 remainder 0
 3 / 2 = 1 remainder 1
 1 / 2 = 0 remainder 1

read remainders bottom-up: 1101 (binary)

1101 binary = D hex   (8+4+0+1 = 13, D = 13)

slides.walkthrough: Divide 13 by 2 repeatedly, recording each remainder. When the quotient hits 0, stop and read the remainders from bottom to top: 1101. Converting 1101 to decimal gives 13, and 13 in hex is the digit D.
slides.narration: Repeated division extracts binary digits as remainders; reading them upward rebuilds the number. Four bits then map to one hex digit.

slides.heading: Grouping bits

diagram.title: Grouping bits
diagram.note: Group from the right. Pad the leftmost group with zeros if it comes up short.

slides.narration: Hex groups bits in fours, octal in threes. Grouping from the right with zero-padding is the whole technique.

slides.heading: Common pitfalls
bullets: Reading remainders top-down instead of bottom-up. The first remainder is the least significant digit: it goes last.
Forgetting that hex A-F are digits, not variables. F simply means 15.
Grouping bits from the left. Always group from the right, padding the leftmost group.
Mixing up 0x and 0 prefixes: 0x means hex, a leading 0 often means octal in code.
slides.narration: The classic errors: reading remainders in the wrong order, grouping from the wrong end, and misreading number prefixes.

slides.heading: Try it: 26 to binary to hex
slides.text: Convert 26 to binary by repeated division, then group into hex. (Answers: 11010 binary, 1A hex.)
slides.narration: Chain both conversions on one number: divide to binary, group to hex. Two techniques, one answer, full confidence.

modules.title: Subnetting
modules.why: IP addresses are 32-bit numbers wearing dotted-decimal clothes. Reading octets, CIDR prefixes, and computing network and broadcast addresses by hand is core to networking, cloud, and security paths.

slides.heading: IPv4 addresses and octets
slides.lede: An IPv4 address is a 32-bit number split into four 8-bit chunks. Learn to see the bits inside the dots.
slides.narration: This lecture dissects IPv4 addresses: 32 bits, four octets, dotted-decimal notation, and the private ranges.

slides.heading: Anatomy of an address
bullets: An IPv4 address is 32 bits long: four groups of 8 bits.
Each 8-bit group is called an octet and holds a value from 0 to 255.
Dotted decimal writes each octet in decimal, separated by dots: 192.168.1.10.
The dots are human convenience. The wire sees 32 bits: 11000000101010000000000100001010.
Private ranges are reserved for internal networks: 10.x.x.x, 172.16.x.x to 172.31.x.x, and 192.168.x.x.
slides.narration: IPv4 is 32 bits in four octets, written dotted-decimal for humans. Private ranges mark addresses that never route on the public internet.

slides.heading: Seeing the bits: 192.168.1.10
slides.walkthrough: Convert each octet with the place-value recipe: 192 is 128+64, so the 128 and 64 bits are on: 11000000. 168 is 128+32+8: 10101000. The 1 and 10 octets convert the same way.
slides.narration: Each octet converts independently with the binary recipe. Reading dotted decimal as four binary bytes is the foundational subnetting skill.

slides.heading: 32 bits, 4 octets

diagram.title: 32 bits, 4 octets
diagram.note: Subnetting is deciding how many of the 32 bits name the network versus the device.

slides.narration: The address is a 32-bit number; octets are just the display format. Subnetting is the art of splitting those 32 bits between network and host.

slides.heading: Try it: convert an octet
slides.text: Convert the octet 168 to binary by hand (place values 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1). Then convert 10. (Answers: 10101000, 00001010.)
slides.narration: Convert two octets by hand. Fluency here makes every later subnetting calculation dramatically easier.

slides.heading: CIDR notation and masks
slides.lede: The /24 in 192.168.1.0/24 says how many bits name the network. Masks are the same idea in 32-bit form.
slides.narration: This lecture explains CIDR prefixes: what /n means, how masks encode it, and how to count usable addresses.

slides.heading: Prefixes and masks
bullets: CIDR notation appends /n to an address: /n means the first n bits identify the network.
The remaining 32 - n bits identify individual devices (hosts) on that network.
A subnet mask writes the same split as 32 bits: n ones followed by zeros, in dotted decimal.
/24 means 255.255.255.0: the first three octets are network, the last octet is hosts.
Usable hosts = 2^(host bits) - 2. Two addresses are always reserved: network and broadcast.
slides.narration: CIDR's slash number splits the 32 bits into network and host portions. Masks write the same split as an address, and the host-bit count determines network size.

slides.heading: Worked: /24 to mask to host count
slides.walkthrough: Write 24 ones then 8 zeros and convert each octet: the full octets become 255, the empty one becomes 0. Eight host bits give 2^8 = 256 addresses; subtract the reserved network and broadcast addresses for 254 usable.
slides.narration: A /24 is the classic example: mask 255.255.255.0, 256 addresses, 254 usable. The minus-two rule accounts for the reserved ends.

slides.heading: Prefix size versus network size

diagram.title: Prefix size versus network size
diagram.note: A bigger prefix number means a smaller network. /30s connect exactly two routers.

slides.narration: Prefix length and network size move in opposite directions. From /8 down to /30, each extra bit halves the network.

slides.heading: Try it: count a /26
slides.text: A /26 has 32 - 26 = 6 host bits. How many usable host addresses does it hold? (Answer: 2^6 - 2 = 62.)
slides.narration: Compute a /26's usable hosts from the formula. Host bits to the power of two, minus two, is the whole calculation.

slides.heading: Network and broadcast, by hand
slides.lede: Given an address and a prefix, you can find the network's first and last address with pencil and paper.
slides.narration: This lecture computes network and broadcast addresses by hand using AND logic, plus the common-masks reference table.

slides.heading: The two reserved addresses
bullets: The network address has all host bits set to 0. It names the network itself.
The broadcast address has all host bits set to 1. It addresses every host at once.
Compute them by ANDing the IP with the mask, bit by bit: 1 AND 1 = 1, anything else = 0.
Usable host addresses run from network + 1 to broadcast - 1.
For /24s the octet math is trivial; the binary method works for every prefix.
slides.narration: Network is host-bits-zero, broadcast is host-bits-one, and ANDing with the mask finds the network. Usable hosts live between the two.

slides.heading: Worked: 192.168.1.75/24

code.code:
IP:        192.168.1.75   (host octet 75 = 01001011)
Mask:      255.255.255.0  (host octet  0 = 00000000)
AND result: 192.168.1.0   <- network address

broadcast: host bits all 1 -> 192.168.1.255
usable range: 192.168.1.1 through 192.168.1.254

slides.walkthrough: AND each IP bit with the mask bit: where the mask is 0, the result is 0 regardless. So the host octet becomes 0 and the network is 192.168.1.0. Flip the host bits to 1 for the broadcast: 192.168.1.255. Everything between is usable.
slides.narration: ANDing zeroes the host octet to reveal the network address; setting host bits gives the broadcast. The usable range is everything in between.

slides.heading: The AND recipe

diagram.title: The AND recipe
diagram.note: AND keeps a 1 only where both bits are 1. Mask zeros erase the host portion.

slides.narration: Four steps find any network and broadcast: write both in binary, AND them, then read the network from zeros and the broadcast from ones.

slides.heading: Common masks reference
slides.walkthrough: Each row halves the previous network: /25 is half a /24, /26 a quarter, and so on. /30's two usable addresses are exactly enough for a point-to-point link between two routers.
slides.narration: This table is worth memorizing from /24 down: each step halves the network, and /30 is the special case for router-to-router links.

slides.heading: Try it: find the network
slides.text: Given 10.0.5.200/24, what is the network address? The broadcast? The usable range? (Answers: 10.0.5.0, 10.0.5.255, .1 through .254.)
slides.narration: Apply the whole recipe to a new address: network, broadcast, and usable range. If all three come easily, subnetting has clicked.

modules.title: Logic & Sets
modules.why: Access rules, firewall policies, database queries, and code conditions are all logic. Sets, truth tables, and De Morgan's laws let you read and simplify them confidently.

slides.heading: Sets and Venn intuition
slides.lede: A set is just a collection of things. Unions, intersections, and complements describe how collections combine.
slides.narration: This lecture introduces sets: membership, union, intersection, and complement, with the Venn intuition behind each.

slides.heading: Set vocabulary
bullets: A set is a collection of distinct things: {1, 2, 3} or {red, green, blue}.
Membership asks is it in there: 2 is in {1, 2, 3}, 5 is not.
Union (A or B) collects everything in either set, with no duplicates.
Intersection (A and B) keeps only what is in both sets.
Complement (not A) is everything outside A, relative to some universe of possibilities.
slides.narration: Sets collect things; union merges, intersection overlaps, complement excludes. These three operations mirror OR, AND, and NOT.

slides.heading: Worked: combining two sets
slides.walkthrough: The union gathers all four distinct numbers. The intersection keeps only 3, the one member they share. Removing B's members from A leaves 1 and 2.
slides.narration: Three operations on the same two sets: union gathers, intersection overlaps, difference excludes. Venn diagrams draw exactly these regions.

slides.heading: The three regions

diagram.title: The three regions
diagram.note: Every WHERE clause, firewall rule, and search filter carves out one of these regions.

slides.narration: Picture two overlapping circles: the union is everything covered, the intersection is the overlap, the complement is the rest of the page.

slides.heading: Try it: overlap
slides.text: A = {a, b}, B = {b, c}. What is the intersection? The union? (Answers: {b}, {a, b, c}.)
slides.narration: Compute an intersection and union by hand. The shared member is the intersection; everything distinct is the union.

lectures.title: AND, OR, NOT and truth tables

slides.heading: AND, OR, NOT and truth tables
slides.lede: Three little words run all of computing's decisions. Truth tables show exactly what each one means.
slides.narration: This lecture defines AND, OR, and NOT with complete truth tables — the reference for every condition you will ever read.

slides.heading: The three operators
bullets: A proposition is a statement that is either true (1) or false (0).
AND is true only when both sides are true. One false input makes the whole thing false.
OR is true when at least one side is true. Only false-false gives false.
NOT flips a value: NOT true is false, NOT false is true.
A truth table lists every input combination and the result. With two inputs there are exactly four rows.
slides.narration: AND needs both, OR needs at least one, NOT flips. Truth tables enumerate every case so nothing is left to intuition.

slides.heading: The complete truth tables
slides.walkthrough: Read row by row: AND has a single 1, only in the 1-1 row. OR has a single 0, only in the 0-0 row. NOT A ignores B entirely and flips A. Memorizing these three columns pays off forever.
slides.narration: Four rows cover every possibility. AND is strict, OR is generous, NOT inverts — and the table proves each claim exhaustively.

slides.heading: Strict versus generous

diagram.title: Strict versus generous
diagram.note: In code, confusing AND with OR is the most common logic bug. The truth table settles it.

slides.narration: AND is the strict gatekeeper, OR the generous one, NOT the reverser. When a condition misbehaves, check which operator you actually wrote.

slides.heading: Try it: evaluate
slides.text: Let A = 1 (true) and B = 0 (false). What is A AND B? A OR B? NOT B? (Answers: 0, 1, 1.)
slides.narration: Evaluate three expressions from the tables. Reading truth tables fluently is the prerequisite for everything that follows.

slides.heading: De Morgan's laws
slides.lede: Negating a combination flips the combination: the opposite of both is at least one failing.
slides.narration: This lecture proves De Morgan's laws with a worked example and shows where they simplify real conditions.

slides.heading: The two laws
bullets: NOT (A AND B) equals (NOT A) OR (NOT B). The opposite of both is: at least one fails.
NOT (A OR B) equals (NOT A) AND (NOT B). The opposite of either is: both fail.
The pattern: distribute the NOT to each side, and flip AND to OR (or OR to AND).
Intuition: to deny both raining and cold, you only need one of them to be false.
These laws simplify negated conditions in code, queries, and firewall rules.
slides.narration: De Morgan's laws push NOT inside parentheses by flipping the operator. The weather intuition — denying both needs only one failure — makes them memorable.

slides.heading: Worked: verifying the first law

code.code:
let A = 1, B = 0

left side:  NOT (A AND B) = NOT (1 AND 0)
                          = NOT 0 = 1

right side: (NOT A) OR (NOT B) = 0 OR 1 = 1

both sides = 1: the law holds for this row
(check the other three rows the same way)

slides.walkthrough: Evaluate both sides with A true and B false. The left side negates the AND; the right side negates each input and ORs them. Both give 1. Repeating for the other three rows completes the proof.
slides.narration: A truth-table check on one row shows the mechanics; all four rows prove the law. Verification beats memorization.

slides.heading: The flip pattern

diagram.title: The flip pattern
diagram.note: Push the NOT inward, flip the operator. That is the entire law in one move.

slides.narration: One move encodes the law: NOT crosses the parentheses and AND becomes OR. The second law is the mirror image.

slides.heading: Try it: simplify
slides.text: Simplify NOT (x > 5 AND y < 3) using De Morgan's law. (Answer: x <= 5 OR y >= 3. Negating > gives <=, negating < gives >=, AND becomes OR.)
slides.narration: Apply the law to a real code condition: negate each comparison and flip AND to OR. This is exactly how professionals simplify tangled conditions.

modules.title: Statistics Foundations
modules.why: Mean, median, variance, and distributions are the language of data. Every data, analytics, and ML path leans on these ideas daily.

slides.heading: Mean, median, and mode
slides.lede: Three ways to say typical — and they disagree exactly when the disagreement matters most.
slides.narration: This lecture defines the three averages, works them on one dataset, and shows when each one lies.

slides.heading: Three typicals
bullets: The mean is the sum divided by the count: the familiar average.
The median is the middle value when the data is sorted. Half the values sit above it, half below.
The mode is the most frequent value: the winner of the popularity contest.
The mean is sensitive to outliers: one billionaire in the room makes the average salary absurd.
The median resists outliers, which is why incomes and house prices are reported as medians.
slides.narration: Mean averages, median middles, mode repeats. Outliers drag the mean but barely touch the median — which is why the choice of average is a real decision.

slides.heading: Worked: one dataset, three answers

code.code:
data: 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 7, 9

sum = 2+4+4+4+5+7+9 = 35
mean = 35 / 7 = 5

sorted: 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 7, 9
median = 4  (the middle of 7 values)

mode = 4  (appears 3 times, more than any other)

slides.walkthrough: Add all seven values for 35, divide by 7 for a mean of 5. The sorted list's middle value is the fourth one: 4. The value 4 appears three times, more than any other, so it is the mode.
slides.narration: One dataset, three summaries: mean 5, median 4, mode 4. Computing all three on the same numbers shows how each summarizes differently.

slides.heading: Which average when

diagram.title: Which average when
diagram.note: Skewed data? Trust the median. Categories? The mode. Clean symmetric data? The mean.

slides.narration: Match the average to the data's shape: the mean for clean symmetric data, the median for skewed data, the mode for categories.

slides.heading: Try it: the outlier test
slides.text: Data: 1, 2, 3, 100. Compute the mean and the median. Which one better represents a typical value? (Mean 26.5, median 2.5 — the median wins.)
slides.narration: One outlier, two very different answers. Feeling the mean get dragged while the median holds steady teaches more than any definition.

slides.heading: Variance and standard deviation
slides.lede: Averages say where data centers. Spread says how much it wanders — and wandering is often the interesting part.
slides.narration: This lecture measures spread: deviations from the mean, variance, and standard deviation, with a full worked example.

slides.heading: Measuring spread
bullets: A deviation is how far one value sits from the mean: value minus mean.
Deviations cancel out when added (positives balance negatives), so we square each one first.
Variance is the average of the squared deviations: the typical squared distance from the mean.
Standard deviation is the square root of variance. It restores the original units.
Bigger standard deviation means more spread: the data is less predictable.
slides.narration: Spread is built in four steps: deviations, squares, average, square root. Squaring stops cancellation; rooting restores units.

slides.heading: Worked: spread of 2,4,4,4,5,7,9

code.code:
mean = 5 (from last lecture)

deviations:  -3, -1, -1, -1, 0, 2, 4
squared:      9,  1,  1,  1, 0, 4, 16
sum of squares = 32
variance = 32 / 7 = 4.57
stddev = sqrt(4.57) = 2.14

slides.walkthrough: Subtract the mean 5 from each value for the deviations. Square each: negatives become positive. Sum the squares (32), divide by 7 for variance (4.57), and take the square root for a standard deviation of about 2.14.
slides.narration: Every step shown: deviations, squares, average, root. A standard deviation of 2.14 means typical values wander about two units from the mean.

slides.heading: The spread recipe

diagram.title: The spread recipe
diagram.note: Squaring stops positives and negatives cancelling. The root converts squared units back to real ones.

slides.narration: Five steps turn raw data into a spread measurement. Each step fixes a problem the previous one created.

slides.heading: Try it: zero spread
slides.text: Data: 5, 5, 5, 5. What is the mean? What is the standard deviation? (Mean 5, stddev 0 — no wandering at all.)
slides.narration: The extreme case teaches the concept: identical values have zero spread. If your calculation gives anything else, recheck the steps.

slides.heading: Distributions: the shape of data
slides.lede: A distribution is the shape data makes when you pile it up. Shape tells you which statistics to trust.
slides.narration: This lecture introduces distributions: the normal bell curve, skew, and uniform shapes, and why shape guides analysis.

slides.heading: Shapes of data
bullets: A distribution shows how values spread out: which values are common, which are rare.
The normal distribution is the famous bell curve: symmetric, with most values near the middle.
Heights, measurement errors, and test scores often look roughly normal.
Skewed distributions have a long tail on one side. Incomes skew right: a few huge values stretch the tail.
In a right-skewed distribution, the mean exceeds the median — the tail drags the average up.
slides.narration: Distributions are data's silhouette: bell curves for symmetric data, skewed tails when outliers stretch one side, flat lines when everything is equally likely.

slides.heading: A histogram, drawn

code.code:
value range | count
 1 - 3      | ##
 4 - 6      | ######
 7 - 9      | ####
10 - 12     | ##

symmetric pile: most values in the middle,
few at the edges -> roughly normal shape

slides.walkthrough: Each # is a data point in that range. The pile is tallest in the middle ranges and tapers at both ends — the silhouette of a bell curve drawn with text.
slides.narration: This text histogram shows a bell shape emerging from raw counts. Reading shapes from histograms is a daily data skill.

slides.heading: Three shapes

diagram.title: Three shapes
diagram.note: Shape tells you which average to trust: symmetric takes the mean, skewed takes the median.

slides.narration: Three archetypes cover most real data: the bell, the skewed tail, and the flat uniform. Name the shape before choosing the statistic.

slides.heading: Try it: pick the average
slides.text: Salaries at a company include one billionaire founder. Should the typical salary be reported as the mean or the median? Why?
slides.narration: Apply shape thinking to a real reporting choice: the skewed tail demands the median. This judgment call appears in every data role.

modules.title: Probability
modules.why: Uncertainty is everywhere in data, ML, and security: test accuracy, model confidence, risk estimates. Sample spaces, independence, and Bayes' rule make uncertainty calculable.

slides.heading: Sample spaces and independent events
slides.lede: Probability is counting: favorable outcomes over possible outcomes. List the possibilities and the math follows.
slides.narration: This lecture defines sample spaces and events, computes simple probabilities, and multiplies independent events.

slides.heading: Probability basics
bullets: A sample space is the set of all possible outcomes of an experiment.
An event is a subset of the sample space: the outcomes you care about.
Probability = favorable outcomes divided by total outcomes (when all are equally likely).
Independent events do not affect each other: one coin flip never remembers the last.
For independent events, P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B). Multiply the chances.
slides.narration: Probability is disciplined counting: list every outcome, count the ones you want, divide. Independence lets you multiply.

slides.heading: Worked: two coin flips

code.code:
sample space: HH, HT, TH, TT  (4 outcomes)

P(two heads) = 1 / 4
P(at least one head) = 3 / 4   (HT, TH, HH)

independent check:
P(head then head) = 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4  (matches)

slides.walkthrough: List all four outcomes first — that is the sample space. Two heads is one of four: probability 1/4. At least one head covers three of four: 3/4. Multiplying the independent single-flip chances gives the same 1/4, confirming independence.
slides.narration: Two methods agree: counting outcomes and multiplying independent chances. When both give 1/4, the model is consistent.

slides.heading: Counting probability

diagram.title: Counting probability
diagram.note: Every probability problem starts by listing the sample space. Skip that step and the counting goes wrong.

slides.narration: The hierarchy of probability: enumerate everything, isolate what you want, divide. Listing first prevents the classic miscounts.

slides.heading: Try it: dice
slides.text: A fair six-sided die: what is P(rolling a 6)? What is P(rolling two sixes in a row)? (Answers: 1/6, 1/36.)
slides.narration: Apply counting and independence to dice. The 1/36 shows how fast combined chances shrink.

slides.heading: Bayes' rule, intuitively
slides.lede: Evidence should update your beliefs — but by how much? Bayes' rule does the accounting, and base rates dominate.
slides.narration: This lecture builds Bayes' intuition with the classic medical-test example, worked with real numbers.

slides.heading: Updating beliefs
bullets: The prior is what you believed before the evidence: how common the condition is.
The evidence is what you observed: a positive test, an alert, a symptom.
The posterior is the updated belief: how likely the condition is, given the evidence.
Rare conditions make most positives false, even with accurate tests. Base rates dominate.
Bayes' rule powers spam filters, medical diagnosis, and fraud detection.
slides.narration: Prior belief meets evidence and becomes posterior belief. The surprise is how much the prior — the base rate — controls the answer.

slides.heading: Worked: the 99%-accurate test

code.code:
1000 people, 1% have the condition, test 99% accurate

sick:    10 people -> true positives:  10 x 0.99 = 10
healthy: 990      -> false positives: 990 x 0.01 = 10

positive test -> P(sick) = 10 / (10 + 10) = 50%

a 99%-accurate test is a coin flip here.
base rates dominate.

slides.walkthrough: Out of 1000 people, 10 are sick and nearly all test positive: 10 true positives. Of the 990 healthy, 1% falsely test positive: about 10 false positives. So a positive result comes from 20 people, only 10 of them sick: 50%.
slides.narration: The arithmetic shocks everyone: a 99%-accurate test is a coin flip when the condition is rare. Counting people instead of trusting percentages reveals why.

slides.heading: Prior to posterior

diagram.title: Prior to posterior
diagram.note: Evidence moved belief from 1% to 50% — a huge update, yet still far from certain.

slides.narration: The test moved the needle enormously — from 1% to 50% — but certainty never arrived. That gap is the base rate talking.

slides.heading: Try it: raise the base rate
slides.text: Same test, but now 50% of 1000 people are sick. Recompute: true positives = 500 x 0.99 = 495, false positives = 500 x 0.01 = 5. What is P(sick) given a positive test now?
slides.narration: Rerun the arithmetic with a 50% base rate and watch the posterior jump to 99%. The test did not change — the prior did.

modules.title: Linear Algebra Essentials
modules.why: Machine learning is linear algebra at scale: data as vectors, transformations as matrices, and the dot product inside every neuron. These essentials demystify ML math.

slides.heading: Vectors and matrices
slides.lede: A vector is a list of numbers; a matrix is a grid of them. Together they are how ML holds data.
slides.narration: This lecture defines scalars, vectors, and matrices, and shows how data becomes vectors.

slides.heading: The three containers
bullets: A scalar is a single number: 5, -3.2, 0. It has magnitude but no direction.
A vector is an ordered list of numbers: [3, 4]. Order matters: [3, 4] is not [4, 3].
The dimension is how many numbers a vector holds. [3, 4] is 2-dimensional.
A matrix is a rectangular grid of numbers with rows and columns. Its shape is rows x columns.
In ML, one data point is often one vector: [height, weight, age] is a 3-dimensional description of a person.
slides.narration: Scalars are single numbers, vectors are ordered lists, matrices are grids. Machine learning stores data points as vectors and datasets as matrices.

slides.heading: Vectors and matrices, written

code.code:
vector v = [3, 4]          (2 dimensions)

matrix M = [[1, 2],
            [3, 4]]        (2 rows x 2 columns)

person = [68, 150, 34]    (height, weight, age)

slides.walkthrough: The vector v holds two numbers, so it is 2-dimensional. The matrix M has two rows and two columns: shape 2x2. The person vector packs three measurements into one ordered list — the standard ML encoding of a data point.
slides.narration: Read the shapes: vector length is dimension, matrix shape is rows-by-columns. Encoding a person as [68, 150, 34] is exactly what datasets do.

slides.heading: Climbing the containers

diagram.title: Climbing the containers
diagram.note: Each level organizes more data. A dataset is a matrix whose rows are data-point vectors.

slides.narration: Each container nests the last: numbers into lists, lists into grids. A dataset is a matrix of row-vectors, one per data point.

slides.heading: Try it: name the shape
slides.text: What is the shape of [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]? How many dimensions does the vector [7, 8, 9, 10] have? (Answers: 2x3, four.)
slides.narration: Read shapes from notation: count rows and columns for matrices, count entries for vector dimension.

lectures.title: The dot product and why ML cares

slides.heading: The dot product and why ML cares
slides.lede: Multiply pairs, add them up: the dot product is simple arithmetic that powers similarity, projections, and neural networks.
slides.narration: This lecture works a dot product by hand and explains why this one operation sits at the heart of machine learning.

slides.heading: The dot product
bullets: The dot product takes two same-length vectors and returns a single number.
Recipe: multiply matching pairs, then add the products.
It measures alignment: large when vectors point the same way, zero when perpendicular, negative when opposed.
A neural network neuron is mostly dot products: inputs dotted with weights, plus a twist.
Similarity search, recommendations, and attention mechanisms all lean on dot products.
slides.narration: Pairwise multiply, then sum: the dot product compresses two vectors into one alignment score. Neurons are built from it.

slides.heading: Worked: [1,2,3] dot [4,5,6]
slides.walkthrough: Pair the first entries: 1x4 = 4. Pair the seconds: 2x5 = 10. Pair the thirds: 3x6 = 18. Add the three products: 4 + 10 + 18 = 32. The two vectors collapse to the single number 32.
slides.narration: Three multiplications and one addition: the dot product of [1,2,3] and [4,5,6] is 32. Every neuron performs this same ritual thousands of times.

slides.heading: Dot product, visualized

diagram.title: Dot product, visualized
diagram.note: Two vectors in, one alignment score out. That score is what neurons, search, and attention all consume.

slides.narration: The dot product is a funnel: two vectors enter, pairwise products form, and a single score exits. Machine learning runs on funnels like this.

slides.heading: Common pitfalls
bullets: Mismatched lengths. The dot product needs equal-length vectors; [1,2] dot [3,4,5] is undefined.
Expecting a vector back. The dot product returns a single scalar, not another vector.
Forgetting order does not matter here: a . b equals b . a. (Matrix multiplication is pickier.)
Confusing dot product with element-wise multiply, which keeps a vector of the pairwise products.
slides.narration: The usual mistakes: mismatched lengths, expecting a vector result, and confusing the dot product with element-wise multiplication.

slides.heading: Try it: compute one
slides.text: Compute [2, 3] dot [5, 7] by hand. (Answer: 2x5 + 3x7 = 10 + 21 = 31.) Then say in one sentence what a large dot product means.
slides.narration: Compute a dot product yourself and interpret it: large means aligned. Arithmetic plus meaning is the complete skill.
